examples.label: Check write access on a specific service pipe

notes:
=== NAMED PIPES ENUMERATION ===
Named pipes are an IPC mechanism often used by services running as SYSTEM.
A writable pipe to a SYSTEM process can enable token impersonation.

ENUMERATION COMMANDS:
pipelist.exe /accepteula                          → list all named pipes
accesschk.exe /accepteula -w \\.\pipe\*         → find writable pipes
accesschk.exe -accepteula -p <PID>               → check process pipe permissions
[System.IO.Directory]::GetFiles('\\\\.\\pipe\\') → PowerShell pipe enumeration

EXAMPLE FINDING: WindscribeService
accesschk on \\.\pipe\WindscribeService showed Everyone:W
This means any user can write to the pipe and send commands to the SYSTEM-level service

=== CHAINING CONTEXT ===
Writable pipe to SYSTEM service → token impersonation or command injection into service context
Named pipe servers can be abused with tools like PipeCapture or custom clients
Potato attacks (JuicyPotato/PrintSpoofer) create named pipes to coerce SYSTEM authentication
PrintSpoofer specifically creates a pipe and coerces Spooler to connect to it

=== WHAT TO LOOK FOR ===
Pipes writable by low-privilege groups (Everyone, BUILTIN\\Users, NETWORK SERVICE)
Custom application pipes (non-Microsoft) — vendor implementations are less hardened
Pipes belonging to services running as LocalSystem

recommended.note: A writable service pipe often means a weak-ACL service.
Local-only service on a pipe/port -> vulnerable-service exploit.

name: WinPE - Named Pipe Enumeration
description: Lists named pipes and their DACLs. A pipe writable by your user (e.g. an insecure service pipe like WindscribeService) can allow impersonation or command execution - see CVE-2020-27350-style abuses.

defense.why_it_works: Named pipes are Windows IPC channels. If a named pipe grants write access to broad groups (Everyone, Authenticated Users) but is owned by a privileged process, an attacker can interact with the pipe to trigger privilege escalation. Enumeration with pipelist.exe and accesschk.exe reveals such misconfigured pipes.
defense.prerequisites: Shell access. Sysinternals PipeList and AccessChk available. Named pipe with weak DACL accessible by the attacker's user.
defense.impact: Identifies named pipe abuse vectors. If a SYSTEM-level service owns a pipe accessible to all users, interaction may trigger token impersonation or other escalation.
defense.detection: pipelist.exe / accesschk.exe execution by non-admin. gci \\.\pipe\ PowerShell command. Unusual process connections to named pipes.
defense.artifacts: Process log: pipelist.exe and accesschk.exe executed | Named pipe access audit events
defense.prevention: Audit named pipe DACLs regularly. Ensure pipes used by privileged services are not accessible to Everyone or Authenticated Users for write. Apply principle of least privilege on pipe security descriptors.
defense.misconfiguration: Third-party application creates a named pipe with write access to Everyone while the owning service runs as SYSTEM (e.g., WindscribeService). No auditing of named pipe ACLs.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Find writable named pipes:
accesschk.exe -w \pipe\* -v
# WindscribeService: \pipe\WindscribeService grants FILE_ALL_ACCESS to Everyone

# Exploit: interact with pipe to escalate via Exploit-DB 48021
defense.secure_config:
# Audit named pipe permissions
accesschk.exe /accepteula \pipe\ -v | findstr 'Everyone\|Authenticated Users'

# Fix overly permissive pipes via application vendor or service configuration
# Restrict pipe DACL to only legitimate client processes
# Monitor: new named pipe creation by non-SYSTEM processes
defense.evasion: Run one consolidated enumeration pass (winPEAS/Seatbelt) in-memory and save output off-host rather than repeated noisy queries.
